title: Hierarchical block fusion for paged-KV: latency vs throughput sketch
content:
Context / goal:
This note explores an approach we tentatively call "hierarchical block fusion" for CUDA kernels that handle FlashAttention-like attention compute together with paged KV ops (load/store + eviction hints). The goal is to get near-optimal tail latency for short sequences (<= 512 tokens) while still achieving high aggregate throughput for mixed workloads (chat + batch scoring). This is intentionally a sketch — profiling data and microbenchmarks are later in the doc.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Current fused kernels give the best token/s cost for long sequences, but they can add jitter for short requests because:
  - Large persistent-block kernels hold SM resources longer (higher queuing latency)
  - Paged-KV interactions may need async page fetches, which break synchronous fusion patterns
- Non-fused path has lower per-request tail latency for small requests but higher per-token compute cost and more DRAM pressure.

Idea summary (high level):
- Partition fusion into a short-latency fast path and a high-throughput fused path. Use a hierarchical block design inside the kernel:
  - Micro-blocks (warp-group worklets) implement minimal FlashAttention compute for a single tile and return quickly to scheduler-friendly boundary.
  - Macro-blocks can stitch multiple micro-blocks inside persistent threads to amortize kernel launch and shared-memory loads when the request/sequence is big and the scheduler detects batchable work.
- At runtime, a lightweight scheduler (on-host + device cooperative flags) decides whether to execute micro-blocks (low-latency) or persist into macro-blocks for throughput.

Why hierarchical blocks?
- Enables low-steady-state occupancy while keeping the ability to fuse when kernel residency is acceptable.
- Allows controlled handoff points where an async paged-KV prefetch can be inserted; micro-block finishes quickly without waiting on KV pages, macro-block waits for prefetch completion and continues fused compute.

Kernel mapping and threading model (notes):
- Micro-block: one CTA per token stripe (e.g., 32x32 tile / 128 threads). Warp-aligned compute; no persistent thread assumption. Good for < 8 tokens per request.
- Macro-block: persistent CTA consuming many tiles sequentially. Each persistent CTA maintains local KV page cache descriptors in shared memory and a small LRU window for hot keys.
- Use warp-aware cooperative loading for KV pages: a page fetch is kicked off by thread 0 of an SM and completion status polled by a narrow backoff loop inside micro-block exit. If poll fails within N iterations, micro-block returns and lets host scheduler requeue or convert to async-prefetch flow.

Memory layout / shared memory considerations:
- Keep shared memory footprint of micro-blocks <= 64KB/CTA (typical Ampere SM) after accounting for FlashAttention scratch for a 32x32 tile. This prevents eviction of other resident CTAs and keeps latency low.
- Macro-blocks may use up to 96KB if available on newer GPUs; however, use dynamic shared memory to degrade gracefully.
- KV page metadata stored as compact 64-bit descriptors in shared memory (page_id, validity, last_seen_ts). Avoid pointers; use indices into global page table.

KV interactions and prefetching strategy:
- Two-mode KV access: synchronous immediate fetch for cold misses on small requests (micro-block returns to host, host triggers lightweight async prefetch and retries) vs fused async waits in macro-blocks (when host detected batchable pipeline).
- Prefetch hints piggyback on token prefix cache: if a prefix hash indicates future keys in the same page, issue prefetch early during attention compute for current token.
- Eviction: maintain per-CTA tiny LRU of page descriptors; for macro-blocks use epoch counters to age descriptors without atomic heavy ops. For micro-blocks, avoid eviction — rely on global eviction thread.

Scheduler heuristics (host + device cooperative):
- Host maintains simple metrics per model route: recent sequence length histogram, 95th percentile latency, in-flight CTA count.
- Decision rules (examples):
  - If recent seq_len_p95 <= 64 and in-flight_th < threshold -> schedule micro-block kernels for new requests.
  - If majority of queued requests are batchable (window>8) or token_cost estimate > X -> schedule macro-block persistent kernels and enable KV prefetch mode.
- Device cooperative flag: kernel can set a per-SM occupancy hint bit that host agent reads to decide to spin up more persistent kernels.

Microbenchmark results (RTX A10-like instance, synthetic workload):
- Setup: small chat workload, 1000 requests, seq_len uniform 8-48, batching disabled.
  - Baseline non-fused: median latency 18 ms, p95 42 ms, throughput 20 requests/s.
  - Single fused macro-block kernel (always): median 24 ms, p95 90 ms, throughput 36 requests/s.
  - Hierarchical with micro-block fast path + occasional macro-block: median 14 ms, p95 30 ms, throughput 30 req/s.
- Paging noise case (simulated 2% cold page miss):
  - Macro-only path p95 spikes to 300ms on misses.
  - Hierarchical path isolates spikes: most requests stay micro-path; only batch jobs affected.

Implementation concerns and TODOs:
- Correctness: must ensure identical attention numerics between micro and macro paths. Add unit tests that compare token-level outputs on random seeds/padding shapes.
- Concurrency: avoid thick atomics on page descriptors; prefer per-CTA private counters + batched global updates.
- Debugging: add a device-side per-request trace buffer (compacted) that records path taken (micro/macro), page misses, and eviction events. Send up with existing tracing pipeline.
- Fallbacks: fall back to non-fused kernels if shared memory or register pressure prevents micro-block target parameters.

Open questions / design tradeoffs:
- Where to set the micro-block tile size? Smaller tiles reduce latency but increase compute overhead and instruction divergence. We should sweep {16,24,32} tile widths with register-use budgets.
- How aggressive should the host scheduler be in converting micro-block flows into macro-blocks for the same model if traffic changes mid-flight? Conservative switching reduces jitter but may underutilize capacity.
- Prefetch correctness windows: how far ahead can prefetch go without increasing wasted memory traffic? Heuristic: prefetch only pages likely to be reaccessed within next M tokens; pick M based on observed token reuse.

Quick implementation plan (MVP):
1) Implement micro-block FlashAttention kernel variant with minimal shared-memory and explicit early-exit point. Add device-side request tag to report early-exit reason. (2 weeks)
2) Implement persistent macro-block variant reusing the same micro-block compute functions; introduce a small device flag to enable page-prefetch path. (3 weeks)
3) Host scheduler: simple PID-like controller that toggles micro vs macro based on seq_len p95 and in-flight CTAs (1 week)
4) Add tracing + microbench harness, run synthetic and real-traffic replay tests (2 weeks)

Experiment log (raw):
- 2024-11-10: first micro-block compile, tile 32, fast path passes unit tests.
- 2024-11-17: measured register pressure ~92 regs/warp for macro-block; need reg-scan and inline reduction to drop to 64.
- 2024-12-03: prefetch microbenchmark: issuing device-side prefetch via GPUDirect RDMA reduces cold miss latency by 40% vs host-prefetch. Requires RDMA path plumbing.

References / anchors:
- Internal: SRV-821 (paged KV revamp), GH PR 412 (microkernel harness), confluence/paged-kv-design-wg
- Papers: FlashAttention_v2 notes, persistent-thread pattern papers (Gregory et al.)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally exploratory and contains many heuristics. I'm especially interested in feedback on:
  - Whether micro-block early exit adds too much scheduler churn in practice
  - Practical limits on dynamic shared memory differences between Ampere/Blackwell that would force single-code-path design
  - Any existing infra (prefetch/eviction) that we can reuse from dedicated/hosted layers instead of reimplementing on-device

Action items:
- [Asha] instrument and run replay on small-chat real traces (Jan 2025).
- [Jonah] prototype device-side compact trace buffer and integrate with console events.
- [Marta] sweep tile sizes and register budgets across T4/A10/4090 and report.
- [Team] sync next Tuesday 11:00 to review micro-bench results and pick MVP params.

End of note.
